title: A family plan for urgent calls
body_md:
## Decide before the phone rings

Nobody works out where the fire exits are while the corridor fills with smoke. You walk them once, on a calm afternoon, so that your feet know the way when your head does not. A family verification plan is the same kind of rehearsal for the call that comes at the worst possible hour: a short agreement made *before* anyone is frightened.

It will not unmask every deepfake, and it does not try to. What it does is give everyone permission to pause, hang up and check by a route chosen in advance. The FTC describes fake-emergency callers who lean on urgency, secrecy, personal details and, sometimes, a cloned voice. The plan works just as well when the caller merely does an impression, or fakes the number on your screen.

### Three rules and a sentence

Begin with the two or three people most likely to get an emergency request. Agree on three rules: no money and no account codes on an incoming call; call the person back on the number you have saved; and if there is no answer, reach another relative, or a real institution through its published number. Decide who will help a young or older relative make that second call. Then rehearse one sentence until it comes without thinking: “I want to help. I am hanging up and calling you on the number I already have.” A real emergency can still be handled quickly, just by a different road.

### The optional phrase

A shared phrase is a reminder, not proof. Pick one that has nothing to do with public birthdays or pet names, and never reuse a password or a one-time account code. Keep the circle small, say when the phrase is meant to be used, and replace it if it leaks. A caller who knows the phrase still gets a callback; a real relative who forgets it still deserves a welfare check. If no phrase suits your family, the callback stands on its own. A fixed renewal date will not make a phrase safe by itself.

### Write the route down

Keep the route written down somewhere safe: saved numbers, a second family contact, and the emergency numbers that apply where you live. Keep secret phrases out of any shared public post. During a call, one person can make the independent callback while another stays ready to seek medical or police help. Afterwards, tell the family what happened, with no blame for whoever took the call. If money has gone, ask the bank or payment provider quickly about recovery, and report through your local channels.

The plan works only if the people who might take such a call know it and have practised it. A few minutes spent rehearsing hang-up and callback beat any attempt to turn everyone into an audio-forensics expert.

widget_config.goal: Agree on a callback plan for urgent requests, rehearse it, and know whom to try next when someone does not pick up.
widget_config.today_action: Ask two people close to you to say aloud, “I will call you back on your saved number,” and save a backup contact.
widget_config.scope: General advice for households, checked 20 October 2026. Adapt the emergency numbers and the payment-recovery steps to your country. A shared phrase is optional and guarantees nothing. The people and calls in the cases are invented.

sources.title: FTC: Scammers Use Fake Emergencies To Steal Your Money
sources.scope: US consumer advice, page dated September 2023: voice cloning, urgency, calling back on a number you know, and checking with another relative. The reporting route it gives applies only in the US.

blocks.title: A “granddaughter” asks you to keep a payment quiet
blocks.situation: A caller says she is your granddaughter. She has been detained, she says, and needs money sent through a new intermediary before anyone else finds out.
blocks.analysis: The demand for secrecy is there to switch off your family network. End the call, dial the saved number, then the agreed backup person. If a genuine detention is possible, contact the relevant local authority yourself, and do not pay the caller’s intermediary.

blocks.title: A real relative forgets the phrase
blocks.situation: After an injury, your uncle phones from the clinic. He cannot recall the optional family phrase, and what he wants is for someone to come and collect him, not a transfer.
blocks.analysis: A forgotten phrase does not make him a fraudster. Ring the clinic on its published number, or another relative, to confirm where he is, then arrange help. The protocol is there to support care, not to block it.

blocks.title: Draw up the family plan
blocks.setup: An invented scene: three relatives are agreeing how to handle an urgent call. One has an old phone and one travels a lot.

steps.prompt: What is the rule for an incoming request for money?

choices.text: End the call and dial the saved number yourself
choices.consequence: Everyone has a simple first move.
choices.explanation: A saved contact lives outside the caller’s story.

choices.text: Ask the caller to text a photo as proof
choices.consequence: A convincing picture arrives, and you still do not know who sent it.
choices.explanation: The caller controls the picture as much as the call.

steps.prompt: The relative who travels may not pick up. Choose the fallback.

choices.text: Call a second agreed relative, or an institution on its published number
choices.consequence: The plan still works with one phone out of reach.
choices.explanation: You can check on someone’s welfare independently, without sending the caller a cent.

choices.text: Treat no answer as confirming the emergency payment
choices.consequence: A phone out of reach turns into false “evidence”.
choices.explanation: Silence has plenty of ordinary causes.

steps.prompt: A relative suggests a shared phrase. How should it be used?

choices.text: As sole proof, in place of the callback
choices.consequence: One overheard phrase can defeat the whole plan.
choices.explanation: A shared secret alone does not verify what is happening now.

choices.text: As an optional clue next to an independent callback
choices.consequence: The phrase helps people remember without taking the place of the callback.
choices.explanation: It can leak or be forgotten; the saved route stays primary.

blocks.debrief: What the family agreed is a short, rehearsed callback with a fallback. A phrase may help, but it never replaces the callback. Go through the choices together, out loud.

questions.prompt: A real relative, injured, cannot remember the family phrase. What do you do?

choices.text: Refuse to help because the phrase is missing
choices.explanation: A phrase is optional and fallible.

choices.text: Confirm through a clinic or another saved contact, then help
choices.explanation: The plan supports a genuine emergency and does not treat a failed memory as guilt.

questions.prompt: Who should know the response plan?

choices.text: Only the person who designed it
choices.explanation: The others need to practise before panic arrives.

choices.text: The people likely to receive or check an urgent request
choices.explanation: A callback fails if only one family member knows about it.

questions.prompt: A caller gives you the phone number of a hospital. What do you do?

choices.explanation: A number supplied by the caller can lead straight to an accomplice.

choices.text: Call it and treat the answer as independent proof
choices.explanation: The number still came from the unverified caller.
